steps.stem: Memory researchers tested a hypothesis by the following experiment. Participants were asked to walk about a room, collect a number of objects scattered in it and place them in a box, which was then sealed. Half of the participants were then asked to remain in the room, and the other half were led to a different room. Finally every participant was asked to name as many of the collected objects as he could. Which of the following hypotheses is the one the researchers tested?
choices: A person is more likely to remember a set of items if he chose them himself than if they were chosen for him
The more items a person stores in memory at one time, the larger the share of them he forgets
A person recalls items better when the recall takes place in the same surroundings in which the items were committed to memory
Concealing objects shortly after they have been seen reduces the chance that they will be remembered
explanation: The only thing that differs between the halves is the room; (1), (2) and (4) name variables the design does not vary.

steps.stem: Researchers hypothesized that giving a large monetary incentive to teenagers who work out at a fitness club would increase their motivation to improve their performance, whereas giving a small monetary incentive would actually lower it. To test their hypothesis, they designed an experiment involving ninety teenagers who work out regularly at a fitness club, who would be divided at random into three equal-sized groups. The participants in the experiment would be asked to lift a light weight as many times as possible within thirty seconds. Every participant in the first group would be offered ten agorot for each time they lift the weight; every participant in the second group – five shekels; and the participants in the third group would not be offered any payment at all. Which of the following is not one of the assumptions that the researchers used when designing the experiment?
choices: When teenagers are presented with a physical challenge with a time limit, they are highly motivated to successfully complete it
It is reasonable to expect that success in lifting light weights reflects success in the various exercises usually done at a fitness club
When participants are divided into groups at random, there are no significant differences in the average level of physical fitness among the groups
The participants would consider ten agorot for each time they lift a weight a small monetary reward, whereas they would consider five shekels a large reward

steps.stem: A study found that the presence of onlookers while a person performs a simple task improves his performance, whereas their presence while he performs a complex task impairs it. Which of the following hypotheses does NOT explain this finding?
choices: Onlookers raise a person's alertness and make him sharper and more focused, which helps in a simple task; but a complex task demands a higher degree of care from the outset, and heightened alertness makes the person nervous and impairs his performance

Onlookers exert pressure that impairs a person's confidence and his ability to complete a task; but the simpler the task, the more confident the person is, and the harmful effect of the onlookers fades

A person wishes to appear in a favorable light and therefore tries to impress the onlookers; the effort helps in a simple task, but in a complex task, which demands much effort in any case, the added effort makes the load too heavy and impairs performance

Onlookers impair a person's concentration on the task; in a complex task this harms performance, but since simple tasks are performed automatically, without much thought, reduced concentration actually helps
explanation: A harm that merely fades cannot produce the improvement observed in simple tasks; (1), (3) and (4) each supply a reason for both halves of the finding.

steps.stem: The researchers Kadmon and Shmida studied the density of the plant malaniel — an annual that blooms in spring and dies in summer — in two habitats of the Judean desert: on the slopes and in the wadis. They found that the density is high in the wadis, and that the difference between the two habitats is not fixed: an increase in rainfall hardly affects the density in the wadis, but leads to a marked rise in density on the slopes. According to their study, if less rain fell in the Judean desert in 2020 than in 2019, it is reasonable that —
choices: the density of malaniel on the slopes in 2020 was higher than in 2019
the gap between the density in the wadis and the density on the slopes was greater in 2020 than in 2019
the density of malaniel on the slopes in 2020 was lower than the density in the wadis in that year
in 2020 the density in the wadis did not change from 2019, but on the slopes it was much higher
explanation: Less rain lowers the slopes and leaves the wadis, so the gap widens. (3) is true in every year and says nothing about the rain; (1) and (4) point the wrong way.

steps.stem: One of the projects that the US National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA) is involved in is the search for life on other planets. Recently, scientists working on this project have become interested in ice cauldrons – cracks in the ice that form distinctive spiral shapes that can be recognized easily even from vast distances. Ice cauldrons are common near Earth's North Pole, and they are formed by the eruption of volcanoes buried under a layer of ice and snow. Tests conducted on Earth show that eruptions like these create an environment that combines heat, humidity and a wide range of minerals. A combination of three of the following claims could explain why NASA is interested in ice cauldrons. Which is the remaining claim?
choices: Since the conditions that cause ice cauldrons to be formed are not unique to Earth, it is possible that cauldrons are also formed on other planets
The combination of heat, humidity and a wide range of minerals is considered ideal conditions for the formation of life
Spiral-shaped cracks in ice could be formed not only by a volcanic eruption, but also by other factors
NASA has almost no other means of searching for life on other planets other than photographing their surfaces from vast distances

steps.title: Scientific reasoning — the words to know
steps.intro: Every study follows one chain: hypothesis → experiment → results → conclusion.

head: Term
What it means
rows: Cause and effect: if X changes, Y changes
X = the factor we change · Y = the result we measure
Groups identical except X — otherwise an alternative explanation
The comparison group: X absent, or X at a different level
The result — supports the hypothesis or contradicts it
Why the results came out as they did

tips: Two question types: understanding the study · understanding the findings.
Assumptions: flip it — if the opposite would ruin the experiment, it's an assumption.
Conclusions given: work out what must follow before reading the choices.
An explanation must cover every part of the finding.

steps.stem: In nature, most things that are blue — the wings of certain butterflies, the feathers of certain birds, the skin of some fish — do not owe their color to a blue pigment; such pigments are rare, and where blue appears it is usually produced by the fine structure of the surface, which is built of layers so thin and so regularly spaced that they reflect blue light and let the other colors pass. The blue dyes used in industry, by contrast, are pigments, and most of them fade in sunlight within a few years. Recently, chemists have succeeded in growing on glass a surface of transparent layers whose spacing matches that of a butterfly's wing, and the glass appears a deep blue although nothing in it is colored. Based on the passage, what new way of producing a blue that does not fade might develop from the chemists' success?
choices: Extracting the rare blue pigments from butterflies' wings and binding them to a surface that protects them from sunlight
Arranging ordinary blue pigments in thin, regularly spaced layers so that they reflect more light and appear deeper in color
Manufacturing surfaces whose transparent layers are spaced so as to reflect blue light, so that the color arises from the structure and not from any pigment
Coating industrial pigments with a layer of glass thin enough to let blue light pass while blocking the light that causes fading
explanation: The discovery is color without pigment; only (3) abandons the pigment. (1) and (2) keep pigments and merely protect or arrange them; (4) protects a pigment rather than replacing it.

steps.stem: In a study, supporters of two rival football clubs were asked a series of questions about historic matches between the clubs, in each of which one club had beaten the other. The study yielded two findings. The first: supporters of the club that had won a given match remembered its course far more accurately than supporters of the club that had lost it. The second: in the years since those matches, supporters of the winning club had watched the recording of the match many more times than supporters of the losing club. What is the relation between the two findings?
choices: The first finding proves the second
The second finding contradicts the first
The second finding supplies an explanation for the first
The first finding describes a general phenomenon, and the second is an instance of it
explanation: Repeated viewing accounts for more accurate memory; the direction runs from the second finding to the first. (2) sees a conflict where there is none; (1) reverses the direction; (4) mistakes two different measures for a general case and an instance.

steps.stem: A researcher compared the prices at which television sets and refrigerators are offered for sale, new and second-hand. She found that the gap between the prices of second-hand television sets bought within the last few years and the prices of new television sets is small, compared with the gap between the prices of second-hand refrigerators of the same age and the prices of new refrigerators. Which of the following facts could explain this finding?
choices: A year ago new refrigerators cost far more than new television sets, but the price of new refrigerators has fallen, and it continues to fall
A new refrigerator of low quality generally costs more than a used refrigerator of high quality, whereas a new television set of low quality generally costs less than a used one of high quality
The quality of a television set deteriorates faster than the quality of a refrigerator
The price of new television sets fell noticeably in the past year, while the price of new refrigerators has hardly changed
explanation: If new sets now cost less than they did, a recent second-hand set is priced against a lower new price, and the gap closes; stable refrigerator prices leave that gap wide. (1) has the wrong appliance falling; (2) describes quality tiers, not the effect of age; (3) would widen the television gap, not narrow it.

steps.stem: Dr. Zohar criticized a study for being irrelevant to its own question, and described it in an analogy: "It is as though you wished to find out whether people who have had cosmetic surgery are pleased with the result, and to that end examined whether cosmetic surgeons suffer from headaches more than other people." Which of the following studies is most likely to be the one Dr. Zohar criticized?
choices: A study that asked whether people who laugh a great deal are happier than others, by comparing the average happiness of professional comedians with that of the general public
A study that asked whether there is a connection between how overweight people believe themselves to be and how overweight they are, by weighing them and questioning them
A study that asked whether medical practice differs between hospitals in the north and the south, by examining patients treated in both
A study that asked whether people who train in a gymnasium grow stronger, by comparing their strength before and after a year of training
explanation: The analogy faults a study for measuring the wrong people (the producers of the thing) on the wrong quantity; comedians stand to laughter as surgeons stand to surgery. (2), (3) and (4) each measure the people the question is about.

steps.stem: Researchers supposed that a plant exposed to frequent touch develops heightened resistance to pests. To test the supposition they grew two seedlings of the same species under identical conditions, except that one was touched frequently and the other not at all, and found that the touched seedling did develop heightened resistance. A chemical test showed that the level of the hormone jasmonate, which is found in plants of every species, was higher in the touched seedling than in the other. The researchers wished to find out whether the hormone is responsible for the heightened resistance, and to that end repeated the experiment with new seedlings, changing one thing. Which of the following is most likely to be the change they made?
choices: They used seedlings that had been genetically altered so as to be unable to produce jasmonate
They scattered a pest-repelling substance around the seedling that was not touched
They used one seedling of the species tested in the first experiment and one of another species
They used two seedlings of the same species, but of a species other than the one tested in the first experiment
explanation: If touched seedlings that cannot make the hormone gain no resistance, the hormone is the link; (2), (3) and (4) change something other than the hormone.

steps.stem: Researchers examined fossilized teeth of people who lived ten thousand years ago and found in them residues of a sedge — a plant that is not a food plant. They noticed that the teeth were remarkably healthy, with almost no cavities, and concluded that people of that period chewed the sedge and that this protected their teeth from decay. Another researcher argued that the finding does not show that the sedge protected the teeth, since people of that period did not eat wheat or refined sugar and therefore had no reason to suffer from decay in any case. Which of the following findings could weaken the other researcher's argument?
choices: Fossils other than teeth showing that people of ten thousand years ago consumed large quantities of the sedge
Fossilized teeth of people who lived at a time when wheat and sugar were already eaten, which contain no residue of the sedge and have more cavities than the teeth the researchers examined
Fossilized teeth of people who lived ten thousand years ago, which contain no residue of the sedge and have more cavities than the teeth the researchers examined
Fossilized teeth of people who lived at a time when other means of protecting the teeth were in use, which contain residue of the sedge
explanation: Same period, same diet, no sedge, more cavities — the diet cannot be the whole explanation. (2) is what the critic would predict; (1) and (4) do not bear on the diet argument.

steps.stem: The female cuckoo lays her eggs in the nests of other birds, among them crows. A study found that crow chicks in a nest that also held a cuckoo chick had a higher chance of survival than crow chicks in a nest without one. The authors supposed that the cuckoo chick secretes a smell that repels predators and so lowers the chance that it or its nest-mates will be eaten. Another researcher supposed instead that the cuckoo chooses in the first place to lay in nests that are relatively safe from predators, so as to improve her chicks' chances. The authors carried out a further test whose results allowed them to confirm one of the two hypotheses. Which of the following tests is most likely to be the one they carried out?
choices: They blocked predators' access to a number of nests and measured the survival of the chicks in them
They measured the survival of crow chicks in nests that held chicks of birds other than the cuckoo
They moved cuckoo eggs into randomly chosen crows' nests and measured the survival of the chicks in them
They measured the survival of the cuckoo chicks themselves, and not only that of the crow chicks that shared their nests
explanation: Random placement removes the cuckoo's choice; if survival still rises, the chick itself is the cause. (1), (2) and (4) do not separate choice from effect.

steps.stem: The bacterium Helicobacter pylori is found in the stomachs of most people, yet only about fifteen percent of its carriers develop a stomach ulcer. Which of the following claims, if true, explains these facts?
choices: The multiplication of the bacterium is the cause of the ulcer
The bacterium often appears in the stomach following the presence of another bacterium, and it is the other bacterium that sometimes causes the ulcer
The bacterium is only one of the factors that lead to an ulcer, but an ulcer cannot develop without it
The presence of the bacterium leads to the appearance of another bacterium, and the two together necessarily cause an ulcer
explanation: A necessary condition that is not sufficient is exactly what a common bacterium and an uncommon disease call for. (1) and (4) would make the ulcer common; (2) removes the bacterium's role altogether.

steps.stem: Do elephants understand the communicative meaning of pointing — a human gesture directing attention toward an object? A new study says they do. The researcher stood before three buckets, all of which contained food, and on each trial pointed at a different one; he found that the elephants tended to turn toward the bucket he pointed at. The researcher argued that the elephants' understanding of pointing was not acquired in the course of the experiment but existed before it, and cited a datum from the experiment in support. Which of the following data is most likely to be the one he cited?
choices: The rate at which the elephants turned toward the bucket the researcher pointed at was no lower at the beginning of the experiment than at its end
Young elephants turned toward the bucket the researcher pointed at more often than old elephants did
At the beginning of the experiment the elephants turned toward each of the three buckets at the same rate
Not all the elephants that took part in the experiment turned toward the bucket the researcher pointed at with the same frequency
explanation: Learning would show as improvement over trials; a flat rate from the first trials argues for a prior ability. (3) would suggest the opposite; (2) and (4) concern differences between elephants, not learning.

steps.stem: A teacher noticed that the pupils who attended the revision lessons she gave before the final examination obtained, on average, higher marks than the pupils who did not attend, and concluded that attending the revision lessons contributed to success in the examination. Which of the following explanations could serve as an alternative to the teacher's?
choices: The revision lessons were based on the material taught in class during the year, so that only pupils who had understood it in class understood the revision as well
The pupils who chose not to attend the revision lessons did so because they believed they already commanded the material
The pupils who chose to attend the revision lessons are the diligent and motivated pupils in any case
The teacher who gave the revision lessons was not the one who had taught the subject during the year
explanation: Diligence explains both attendance and marks. (2) would predict high marks for the absentees, the reverse of the finding; (1) and (4) do not explain the gap.

steps.stem: A study of forest areas in Africa that had burned found that in the first years after a fire the trees grow quickly, and that the growth slows later. Dr. Bentzur argued that the charcoal produced by the fire is the cause. Which of the following findings does NOT strengthen Dr. Bentzur's claim?
choices: Charcoal in the soil speeds the development of the grasses that compete with the trees for nutrients
Charcoal neutralizes organic substances in the soil that inhibit the bacteria the trees need for their growth
Researchers who sowed tree seeds in soils mixed with charcoal found that the fresher the charcoal, the better the germination
In burned forests where the charcoal was washed away by rain soon after the fire, no rapid growth was observed
explanation: Helping the trees' competitors would slow the trees, not speed them; (2) supplies a mechanism, (3) the fading of the effect, and (4) the absence of the effect without the cause.

steps.stem: Tree borers are larvae that live inside the trunks of trees, and they are very difficult to eradicate with pesticides. Nevertheless, many farmers succeed in getting rid of them by irrigating the trees with salt water. Which of the following data could explain why irrigation with salt water is effective against tree borers?
choices: The chemical reaction between salt and pesticides lowers the concentration of the pesticides in the trunk without impairing their effectiveness
Salt impairs the reproduction of the tiny insects that feed on the borers
Salt water causes the trees to draw up from the soil certain minerals, near which the borers cannot survive
Salt water costs far less than most of the pesticides on the market
explanation: Only (3) connects the salt to the death of the borers. (2) would help them; (1) and (4) are about pesticides and cost.

steps.stem: In a study, Israeli-born participants were divided into two groups. Group A was asked to memorize a list of names of Israeli towns, group B a list of names of Hungarian towns. When asked to recall the lists, group A remembered many more names. The researcher attributed the difference mainly to group A's familiarity with the names, but raised a second possibility as well: that the result stemmed from the words group B had to remember being Hungarian, and therefore hard for Israelis to pronounce. She therefore conducted a second experiment, whose result showed that the second factor is of secondary importance. Which of the following is most likely to be the result of the second experiment?
choices: Israeli newsreaders who were asked to pronounce foreign words in a broadcast did better with words they had never met before
Hungarian participants remembered lists of Hungarian names better than lists of Israeli names
Hungarian participants remembered lists of everyday Hungarian words better than lists of rare Hungarian words, even when the two lists were equally easy to pronounce
Israeli chemists remembered lists of rare Hebrew words less well than lists of names of molecules that were hard for them to pronounce — provided the molecules were ones they work with
explanation: Familiar-but-hard-to-pronounce beats unfamiliar-but-easy: the pronunciation factor is directly outweighed. (3) shows familiarity matters but does not rank it against pronunciation; (2) repeats the first experiment in reverse; (1) is about pronunciation alone.

steps.stem: At a certain university, most of the men who applied for doctoral studies were accepted, whereas only a minority of the women who applied were accepted. An examination by department, however, found that in every department the proportion of men accepted among the men who applied equaled the proportion of women accepted among the women who applied. Which of the following facts could explain these data?
choices: Most of the men applied to departments that are easy to enter, and most of the women to departments that are hard to enter
Most of the men applied to departments that are hard to enter, and most of the women to departments that are easy to enter
Every department received the same number of applications from men and from women
Most of the men and most of the women applied to the same departments
explanation: Equal rates within departments and unequal rates overall require the two groups to be distributed differently across departments with different acceptance rates — in the direction of (1). (2) gives the wrong direction; (3) and (4) would make the overall rates equal.

steps.stem: A certain starch has a curious property: mixed with a little water it forms a liquid, but a hard stir turns the liquid instantly into a solid. At first the water molecules coat the starch molecules like a lubricant and let them slide past one another; under hard stirring, however, the starch molecules collide and, because of their rough surfaces, lock together into long tangled chains held by friction, and a solid results. When the stirring stops the chains break and the mixture is liquid again. In most other liquids of this class nothing of the kind happens. Which of the following explanations concerning the molecules of the other liquids best fits the passage?
choices: Water does not serve them as a lubricant
When they are stirred hard they do not join together into a solid
The chains they form break when the stirring stops
Their surfaces are not rough
explanation: The passage names the roughness as what makes the molecules lock; its absence is the explanation. (2) restates the difference instead of explaining it; (3) is true of the starch too; (1) would leave the mixture solid from the start.

steps.stem: A study of near-sightedness in children found that the more time children spend out of doors, the less likely they are to become near-sighted. It was also found that among children who had already become near-sighted, the eyesight of those who spend more time out of doors deteriorates more slowly than that of the others. Which of the following can explain the study's findings?
choices: Children who become near-sighted and need to wear glasses tend to spend less time out of doors than children who do not wear glasses
Adults spend less time out of doors than children, and are more likely than children to become near-sighted
Children who spend a great deal of time out of doors read less than other children, and the more a person reads the more his eyesight deteriorates
Exposure to sunlight for many hours is liable to damage the eyes and lead to near-sightedness
explanation: A mechanism that acts on everyone explains both the lower incidence and the slower deterioration. (1) is reverse causation, and it explains only the first finding; (2) is about adults; (4) predicts the opposite.

steps.stem: In September 1967 the traffic laws of Sweden were changed, and motorists began to drive on the right side of the road instead of the left. The change was expected to make driving safer, since the steering wheel in most cars in Sweden was on the left, which suits driving on the right. And indeed, in the first months after the change the rate of road accidents in Sweden fell markedly. But the fall was only temporary, and two years later the rate of accidents had returned to its former level. Which of the following best explains why the fall in the rate of accidents was temporary?
choices: In 1967 Sweden began importing fewer cars with the steering wheel on the right, and in 1969 it stopped importing them altogether
Driving on the right allowed drivers to sit on the left side of the car, and so to see the road better
In 1967 the speed limit on Sweden's highways was raised by ten kilometers an hour
After the change, drivers were especially cautious because they were not yet used to driving on the right
explanation: Caution that wears off explains a fall that reverses. (2) would predict a lasting fall; (1) points the same way; (3) has the wrong timing to explain a fall followed by a return.

steps.stem: Until the 1980s the medical community believed that the acidity of the stomach was too high for bacteria to survive in it, and that bacteria therefore could not be the cause of stomach ulcers. A scientific experiment disproved this assumption. Which of the following CANNOT be that experiment?
choices: Taking a sample of stomach tissue from people suffering from an ulcer, and checking whether bacteria are present in it
Creating an artificial environment with an acidity similar to the stomach's, and checking whether any bacteria survive in it
Treating a stomach ulcer with a medication whose only effect is to kill bacteria, and checking whether the ulcer is cured by the treatment
Using antacids to lower the acidity of the stomach, and checking whether bacteria are present in the stomach after the acidity has been lowered
explanation: Finding bacteria in a stomach whose acidity has been lowered says nothing about whether they survive at the stomach's natural acidity — the assumption at issue. (1), (2) and (3) each could show bacteria present or active under the natural conditions.

steps.stem: Erez boasted to Gadi that he could tell the number of leaves on any bush at a glance. To prove it he pointed at a nearby bush and declared that it had exactly 373 leaves. Gadi, unconvinced, wished to put the claim to the test; but an exact check would have meant counting every leaf on the bush, a long and tiring task, and so he devised a far simpler test. Which of the following is most likely to be the test Gadi devised?
choices: Erez will say how many leaves he thinks are on one half of the bush and how many on the other half, and Gadi will check whether the two figures add up to 373
A passer-by will also say how many leaves he thinks are on the bush, and Gadi will compare his figure with Erez's

Gadi will pick a few leaves off the bush without telling Erez how many he has picked; Erez will say how many leaves are now on the bush, and Gadi will check whether the difference equals the number he picked
Erez will say how many leaves he thinks are on a similar-looking bush; Gadi will count the leaves on that bush and compare
explanation: A genuine ability would track a change whose size only Gadi knows; a guess would not. (1) can be made consistent by anyone, (2) compares two guesses, (4) is the full count Gadi wished to avoid.

steps.stem: Two findings emerged from a study of how readers are affected by the typeface of a printed text: people who read texts printed in a hard-to-read typeface remembered them better than people who read similar texts in an easy-to-read typeface; and people who read instructions printed in an easy-to-read typeface were more willing to follow them than people who read the same instructions in a hard-to-read typeface. On the basis of these findings the researchers drew up a number of recommendations. Which of the following is LEAST likely to be one of them?
choices: Notices in public transport, such as "Do not put your feet on the seats," should be printed in an easy-to-read typeface
The worse a person's memory, the more important it is for him to read texts printed in an easy-to-read typeface
The typeface of a text should be chosen according to the purpose the text is meant to serve
Actors who wish to memorize a text should read it in a hard-to-read typeface
explanation: The first finding links the hard typeface with better memory; (2) sends the person with the weakest memory to the typeface that helps memory least. (1), (3) and (4) follow directly.

steps.stem: The parasite that causes sleeping sickness is carried from one person to another by the tsetse fly, an insect common in tropical Africa. When a tsetse fly bites a person who has the disease, the parasite passes into the fly's body and multiplies there. If one fly bites several people who have the disease and takes up parasites from each of them, genetic material can pass between the parasites while they are in the fly's body; this increases the genetic variety of the parasites and may make them more resistant to medication. According to the passage, which of the following is a likely explanation for the fact that in certain regions the parasites are especially resistant to medication?
choices: In those regions a smaller proportion of the tsetse flies carry the parasite
In those regions there are more tsetse flies
In those regions there is a greater probability that genetic material will pass from the fly's body to the parasite
In those regions there is a greater probability that a fly will bite several people who have the disease
explanation: Resistance follows from exchange between parasites from different hosts, which needs one fly biting several sick people. (2) is a step short; (1) points the other way; (3) misplaces the exchange.

steps.stem: In an experiment, researchers gave yellow teddy bears to children. After a while they offered each child to exchange his bear for one that had been given to another child and was green. Most of the children refused. The researchers supposed that the refusal stemmed from a preference for the color yellow, but a follow-up experiment showed that the supposition was not correct. Which of the following best describes the follow-up experiment?
choices: The researchers gave each child a yellow bear, and after a while offered to exchange it for a smaller green bear; most of the children refused
The researchers gave each child an orange bear, and after a while offered to exchange it for a larger yellow bear; most of the children agreed
The researchers gave each child a yellow bear, and after a while offered to exchange it for a larger yellow bear; most of the children agreed
The researchers gave each child a green bear, and after a while offered to exchange it for an identical bear that was yellow; most of the children refused
explanation: If the children refuse a yellow bear in favor of the green one they already hold, the color preference cannot be the reason. (1) and (2) are consistent with a preference for yellow; (3) does not test color at all.

steps.stem: Two experiments are described. Experiment 1: researchers supposed that drinking twice the usual daily quantity of water improves health. They recruited participants whose health was similar and who habitually drank the average daily quantity, asked them to drink twice that quantity for a month (group A), and at the end of the month compared their health with that of a group who had not changed their habits (group B). Experiment 2: researchers supposed that giving up sugar causes headaches. They asked half of their participants to give up sugar for a week and the other half to go on consuming it as usual, and at the end of the week compared the two halves. Four correspondences between elements of the two experiments follow. Which of them is correct?
choices: Group A in experiment 1 corresponds to the participants who did not give up sugar in experiment 2
Drinking twice the quantity of water in experiment 1 corresponds to giving up sugar in experiment 2
The quantity of water drunk by the members of group A in experiment 1 corresponds to the quantity of sugar consumed by the participants who did not give up sugar in experiment 2
A participant in experiment 1 who did not double his water corresponds to a participant in experiment 2 who gave up sugar
explanation: The change imposed is the change imposed. (1) and (4) pair a changed group with an unchanged one; (3) pairs the manipulated quantity with the untouched one.

steps.stem: The supposition tested in experiment 1 above was not confirmed, whereas the supposition tested in experiment 2 was confirmed. Which of the following recommendations is best supported by the results of the two experiments?
choices: It is worth drinking twice the usual daily quantity of water, and there is no danger in giving up sugar
It is worth drinking twice the usual daily quantity of water, and it is not worth giving up sugar
There is no need to drink twice the usual daily quantity of water, and there is no danger in giving up sugar
There is no need to drink twice the usual daily quantity of water, and it is not worth giving up sugar
explanation: Unconfirmed: no reason to double the water. Confirmed: giving up sugar causes headaches — not worth it.

steps.stem: Researchers showed participants photographs of a dog's face in different emotional states — joy (on receiving a treat), sadness (on being scolded by its owner), fear (on meeting a threatening dog) — and asked them to say which emotion the dog was expressing in each photograph. They found that most participants identified the dog's emotional state well, and that participants who owned dogs succeeded better than the others. Which of the following conclusions best fits the findings?
choices: People are able to identify the facial expressions of dogs, and this ability improves with daily contact with dogs
Dog owners identify the expressions of their own dog well, but not the expressions of other dogs
Some people who have never had contact with dogs can identify their expressions, and some acquire the ability only after prolonged contact
People who have no daily contact with dogs find it hard to identify dogs' expressions
explanation: Most succeeded, owners more; (4) contradicts the first finding, (2) and (3) add distinctions the study did not draw.

steps.stem: In an experiment, participants were asked about their positions on various subjects, and then received fictitious feedback on their answers: some were told that most of the participants had given answers similar to theirs, and others that only a few had. At the end the participants were asked questions designed to reveal their mood. Which of the following is most likely to have been the purpose of the experiment?
choices: To examine the effect of mood on the tendency to express widely held positions
To examine whether people prefer to feel unique or to feel similar to others
To examine whether under experimental conditions people try to express widely held positions
To examine how expressing positions on various subjects affects mood
explanation: The only thing manipulated is the feedback about similarity, and the only thing measured afterwards is mood. (1) reverses the order; (3) and (4) name variables the design does not isolate.

steps.stem: The poet Dana Gioia wrote: "We are in a strange state — although more bad books of poetry are published in the United States today than ever before, most of the reviews of poetry that are published are favorable." Which of the following data could explain the state Gioia describes?
choices: Critics of poetry often disagree about what good poetry is
Critics of poetry prefer not to write reviews of books they find unappealing
Most critics of poetry believe that bad books of poetry should be reviewed harshly, in order to educate readers
In Gioia's time more reviews of poetry are published than in earlier times
explanation: Reviews written only of the books critics like will be favorable however many bad books exist. (3) predicts the opposite; (1) and (4) do not explain the tilt.

steps.stem: In an experiment, two groups of participants watched a film and were asked to rate it according to several professional criteria. While group A watched, a loud noise was played in the adjoining room; group B watched in silence. In the second stage, after they had given their ratings, the members of group A were asked whether they thought the noise had disturbed their judgment, and if so, how. Most of them rated the disturbance as strong and said that it had led them to rate the film lower than they otherwise would; but in fact the ratings given by group A were higher than those given by group B. Which of the following is most likely to have been the purpose of the experiment?
choices: To examine whether people rate their own judgment as better than that of others
To examine whether people assess correctly how disturbances affect their judgment
To examine whether hearing noise leads to harsher judgment than judgment in quiet conditions
To examine whether a lack of attention causes people to rate a film higher
explanation: The second stage asks the participants what the noise did, and the two groups' ratings show what it did; the comparison between the two is the point. (3) is only the second half; (1) and (4) are not tested.

steps.stem: In the cosmetics department of the "Kolbo" store two beauty consultants work, one in the first half of the week and the other in the second half. Recently the manager of the department told the consultant of the first half that he intends to replace him, since the department's sales on the days he works are lower than its sales on the other days. The consultant argued that the low sales are not his fault, and proposed a test to the manager. Which of the following is most likely to be the test the consultant proposed?
choices: To check whether the products in the cosmetics department have recently become more expensive
To check whether the store has recently been short of cosmetic products in high demand
To check whether in other departments of the store, too, there are salespeople who work only in the first half of the week or only in the second
To check whether in the other departments of the store, too, sales in the second half of the week are higher than in the first
explanation: If the whole store sells more late in the week, the days explain the gap, not the consultant. (1) and (2) would affect both halves alike; (3) is about staffing, not sales.

steps.stem: Researchers studied the coral reefs of the Caribbean and were surprised to discover that the place of the "floating corals," which had dominated the reefs for millions of years and had died out in recent decades because of a parasite that attacked them, had been taken over by a population of "brown corals." Which of the following data CANNOT explain why the researchers were surprised?
choices: The floating corals thrive in conditions very different from those in which the brown corals thrive
Most floating corals do not fall victim to parasites
The brown corals are common mainly in cold regions, whereas the Caribbean Sea is warm
The parasite that attacked the floating corals harms every kind of coral
explanation: The surprise is at the takeover, not at the extinction; (2) bears on the extinction alone. (1), (3) and (4) each make the brown corals' arrival unexpected.

steps.stem: A study found that people who often listen to Indian music obtain, on average, higher marks in mathematics tests than people who listen to it rarely. The researchers concluded that listening to Indian music develops mathematical ability. Which of the following could serve as an alternative explanation of the study's findings?
choices: The disposition to develop mathematical ability is innate, whereas a liking for Indian music is not
People with mathematical ability enjoy Indian music more, since they grasp its complex structure
People who listen to music of any kind obtain higher marks in mathematics tests
Listening to Indian music develops the regions of the brain responsible for mathematics
explanation: Ability leads to the listening, not the reverse. (4) is the researchers' own explanation; (1) and (3) do not explain the specific correlation.

steps.stem: A student wished to examine whether the rise in the number of people admitted to hospital in spring is caused by allergic reactions to the blossoming of that season. He gathered a sample of people admitted to hospital in spring and checked how many of them had been exposed to blossoming shortly before. In order that the results should be unambiguous, he needs a further check to compare them with. Which of the following checks is best suited for this?
choices: Among people who were not exposed to blossoming at that time, what proportion were admitted to hospital in spring
Among people admitted to hospital in spring, what proportion were exposed to blossoming only after their admission
Among people exposed to blossoming at that time, what proportion were not admitted to hospital in spring
Among people admitted to hospital in spring, what proportion were exposed to blossoming
explanation: The rate among the unexposed is the baseline the exposed must exceed. (4) repeats his own check; (2) and (3) do not supply a comparison group.

steps.stem: Yossi argues that adults encourage boys and girls, at times without noticing, to behave according to what is regarded as "masculine" and "feminine" behavior, and that this is one of the causes of the differences in inclination between boys and girls. Tali, by contrast, argues that adults only respond spontaneously to the different wishes of boys and girls, which stem from innate natural inclinations. Which of the following studies could help to decide between the two claims?
choices: Observing adults playing with an infant dressed in clothes that do not reveal its sex, and comparing their behavior when they are told it is a boy with their behavior when they are told it is a girl
Observing children of both sexes and checking to what extent they engage in activities regarded as typical of their sex
Following the toys that parents buy for their children according to the children's sex
Interviewing children and asking them whether they are aware of stereotypes about boys and girls
explanation: With the same infant, any difference in the adults' behavior comes from the label, not from the child's inclinations. (2), (3) and (4) cannot separate the two explanations.

steps.stem: Researchers presented two groups of participants with a story about a man who ate in a restaurant and, after receiving a bill of 97 shekels, answered a telephone call and left without paying. Group A was told that the call had distracted him and that this was why he left without paying; group B was told that he had intended from the start not to pay. The researchers supposed that the more a person is perceived as guilty, the more one tends to remember the facts of the case in a way that intensifies the severity of his act. Which of the following findings supports the researchers' supposition?
choices: When asked to recall the name of the restaurant, more members of group A than of group B remembered it
When asked their opinion of the price of the meal, most of group A thought 97 shekels exaggerated, and most of group B thought it fair
When asked whether the story mentioned that the caller was the man's sick mother, more of group B than of group A answered yes
When asked to note the amount of the bill, group A gave on average a sum well below 97 shekels, and group B a sum of about 97 shekels
explanation: The guiltier man is remembered as having left a larger bill unpaid. (3) would soften his act; (1) and (2) do not bear on severity.

steps.stem: In a study, researchers followed a group of African mongooses and found that while the group forages, one of them stands guard in a prominent position, and when it identifies a predator it warns the group with special calls. In a further study the researchers gave extra food to some of the mongooses, and found that they devoted more hours to standing guard than did the mongooses that received no extra food. Which of the following conclusions does the further study support?
choices: An individual's readiness to contribute to the group grows once its own needs have been met
Hunger increases an individual's readiness to endanger itself and to stand guard
Foraging increases an individual's risk of being preyed on
An individual's wish to guard its companions stems from its strong wish to satisfy other needs, such as eating
explanation: More food, more guarding. (2) reverses the finding; (3) and (4) are not tested.

steps.stem: The teacher Sara found that the marks of the pupils who attended the preparation lessons for the mathematics examination were higher on average than the marks of the pupils who did not attend, and concluded that the preparation lessons helped the pupils who attended them. The teacher Dina holds that there is another explanation for the difference between the averages: the better pupils are the ones who chose to attend the preparation lessons, and since they are good pupils they did better in the examination. Which of the following conclusions could be undermined by an alternative explanation of the kind Dina proposed?
choices: Datum: the general health of people who habitually eat organic food is better, on average, than that of people who do not. Conclusion: eating organic food improves health
Datum: a survey among the customers of the clothing chain "Beged-Li" found that it is the cheapest chain in the market. Conclusion: there is no chain cheaper than "Beged-Li"
Datum: infants who received an experimental vaccine, given at random to every fifth infant, fell ill less on average than infants who did not receive it. Conclusion: the vaccine is effective
Datum: people who smile a great deal are happier, on average, than people who smile little. Conclusion: a person who smiles more than another is probably also happier
explanation: People who choose organic food may be the health-conscious to begin with — self-selection, as in Dina's explanation. (3) is randomized; (4) draws no causal conclusion; (2) is a different flaw.

steps.stem: It was found that the group that read text A and then text B rated Ziv's diligence lower than the group that read the texts in the reverse order. This finding —
choices: neither strengthens nor weakens the second hypothesis
weakens the second hypothesis
weakens the first hypothesis and strengthens the second
strengthens both hypotheses
explanation: If earlier information weighed more, the group that met "diligent" first would rate diligence higher; it rated it lower, so the later text weighed more.

steps.stem: If both hypotheses are correct, which group's average rating of Ziv's diligence is expected to be the LOWEST?
choices: The group that read text A only
The group that read text B only
The group that read text A first and then text B
The group that read text B first and then text A
explanation: Only the lazy text, with nothing to raise it; both mixed groups receive some diligent information, which by the first hypothesis affects the rating.

steps.stem: Barak gave Michal a gift. In response, Michal said to Barak: "You gave me a gift to make me happy, but you achieved the exact opposite result." A combination of three of the following facts explains Michal's response. Which is the remaining fact?
choices: Michal can read only Hebrew, French and English
Receiving a gift that she cannot use makes Michal sad
Michal's favorite books are poetry books
Barak gave Michal a thriller written in Spanish. Verbal Reasoning – First Section - 8 - Summer 2024

steps.stem: In an experiment, participants were asked to wait in a university lecturer's office. After a few minutes, they were led into another room, where they were asked to list all the items they had seen in the lecturer's office. Some of them mentioned items, such as books, that were not even in the office. The researchers explained this by hypothesizing that human memory is based on absorbing only a few details and on completing the picture through expectations based on previous experience or on commonplace images. Which of the following can be best explained in the same way?
choices: A person bought a certain TV model, and was later asked which other models were in the store, and remembered them all
A person witnessed a bank robbery, and stated that the robber was carrying a gun, whereas in actual fact the robber was armed only with a knife
A person was involved in a car accident for the first time, and remembered that the car that collided with them was green, whereas in actual fact it was blue
A person attended a wedding, and estimated that there were about one hundred guests there, and indeed, there were exactly one hundred and two guests in attendance
